commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether AI privacy and data governance policies, with requirements traceable to controls, reduce privacy harms in health care. The recommendation rests on the agreement of frameworks, professional guidance, and commentaries rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The support comes from two CHAI frameworks rated must, four guidance documents, and six commentaries. Expert agreement of this kind cannot be graded for certainty of effect, so the rating is no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures how often AI privacy failures occur or whether governance policies catch them before patient data is exposed. The radiology multi-society statement names discrimination, insurance costs, and humiliation as possible harms. Those harms remain unquantified in this evidence set.

Several endorsing sources tie data governance to existing law, citing HIPAA and, in one case, GDPR. This suggests organizations may already hold privacy controls that AI-specific policies could map onto. No supplied study shows whether this mapping reduces violations or enforcement actions.

The CHAI playbook states that full DICOM tag scrubbing requires specialized tools rather than general de-identification methods. FUTURE-AI lists access control and logging as mechanisms. No supplied study reports how well these controls perform in routine workflows or what staff burden they add.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without AI-specific data governance policies and traceable controls, and that measure privacy incidents, re-identification events, unauthorized access, and staff effort. Evaluations of specific controls, such as DICOM de-identification tools and access logging for AI systems, would also help.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence cannot show whether governance policies protect these groups equally. It also cannot show whether the consumer disclosures that RUAIH recommends reach patients with limited English or low literacy.
